objectives: Contrast accrual-basis and cash-basis accounting and explain why accrual provides a truer economic picture.
Apply the five-step ASC 606 / IFRS 15 revenue recognition model to a realistic contract.
Record deferred revenue, accrued revenue, and subscription revenue amortisation using correct journal entries.

slides.title: Accrual vs. cash basis — why timing matters
slides.body:
At the heart of all modern financial reporting lies a fundamental choice: **when** do you recognise revenue and expenses? Two systems exist: **cash-basis accounting** and **accrual-basis accounting**.

**Cash-basis accounting** is simple: record revenue when cash is received; record expenses when cash is paid. A freelancer who invoices a client in November but gets paid in February reports the income in February. A small retail shop that buys inventory in December on credit records the expense only when it pays in January. Cash basis is permissible for small businesses (in the US, the **IRS** allows many firms with average annual gross receipts below $29 million as of 2023 to use cash basis for tax purposes under **IRC Section 448**), and it has the virtue of closely tracking actual cash flow.

**Accrual-basis accounting** is the foundation of financial reporting under both **US GAAP** (governed by the **Financial Accounting Standards Board**, or **FASB**, a private-sector standard-setter established in **1973**) and **IFRS** (governed by the **International Accounting Standards Board**, or **IASB**, established in **2001** as successor to the IASC). Under accrual, revenue is recognised when **earned** — when the company has delivered the goods or services it promised — regardless of when cash changes hands. Expenses are recognised in the same period as the revenue they helped generate.

This principle of **expense matching** is called the **matching principle**: expenses should be matched to the revenues they produced in the same period. It is one of the oldest concepts in accounting, appearing in discussions by accounting theorists like **William Andrew Paton** (1889–1991) and **A.C. Littleton** (1886–1974), whose collaborative 1940 monograph *An Introduction to Corporate Accounting Standards* (published by the **American Accounting Association**) remains a foundational text in accounting theory.

**Why accrual gives a truer economic picture.** Consider a construction company that signs a two-year $10 million contract in January 2024. Under cash basis, if the customer pays 80% upfront, the company records $8 million income in 2024 even though the work spans two years — wildly overstating 2024 performance. Under accrual, revenue is matched to work completed. The income statement reflects economic reality: what was *earned*, not what was *collected*.

Conversely, a retailer that orders $500,000 of inventory in December on net-30 terms has incurred the cost in December — even if cash doesn't leave until January. Accrual captures this correctly; cash basis does not.

The gap between net income (accrual) and cash from operations (the **Statement of Cash Flows**) is precisely the reconciliation that the **indirect method** cash flow statement performs. Analysts at firms like **Goldman Sachs** and **JPMorgan** study this gap as a key indicator of earnings quality.

slides.title: Revenue recognition — ASC 606 and the five-step model
slides.body:
Revenue recognition — **when** exactly a company may record revenue — was one of the most contentious and abused areas of accounting for decades. Many of the biggest accounting scandals of the late 1990s and 2000s involved improper revenue recognition: **Xerox** (2002) improperly accelerated equipment lease revenues; **Lucent Technologies** (2000) recognised revenue on sales where the customer had the right to return goods; **HealthSouth** (2003) fabricated revenues outright. The old standard, **SOP 97-2** for software and **SAB 101** for other industries, had become a patchwork of narrow, industry-specific rules.

In response, the **FASB** and **IASB** undertook a decade-long joint project to replace all existing revenue guidance with a single, principles-based standard. The result:
- **ASC 606** — *Revenue from Contracts with Customers* (US GAAP), effective for public companies for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2017.
- **IFRS 15** — *Revenue from Contracts with Customers* (IFRS), effective for annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2018.

Both standards adopt an identical **five-step model**:

**Step 1 — Identify the contract with a customer.** A contract exists when the parties have approved it, each party's rights are identifiable, payment terms are defined, the contract has commercial substance, and collection is probable.

**Step 2 — Identify the performance obligations in the contract.** A **performance obligation** is a promise to transfer a distinct good or service (or a bundle of goods/services) to a customer. A phone manufacturer selling a handset plus a 2-year service plan has *two* performance obligations: (a) the phone and (b) the service.

**Step 3 — Determine the transaction price.** The amount the company expects to be entitled to in exchange for transferring the goods or services. Includes **variable consideration** (rebates, discounts, bonuses), the **time value of money** (if the contract has a significant financing component), **non-cash consideration**, and **consideration payable to the customer** (e.g. coupons).

**Step 4 — Allocate the transaction price to performance obligations.** If multiple performance obligations exist, allocate the transaction price proportionally based on **standalone selling prices (SSP)**. If the phone sells for $800 standalone and the service plan for $200, an $800 bundled price would be allocated 80% ($640) to the phone and 20% ($160) to the service.

**Step 5 — Recognise revenue when (or as) each performance obligation is satisfied.** Revenue is recognised:
- **At a point in time** — when control transfers to the customer (typical for product sales).
- **Over time** — when the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefit, the company creates an asset the customer controls, or there is no alternative use and the company has an enforceable right to payment for work to date (typical for construction contracts, subscriptions, long-term service agreements).

ASC 606 / IFRS 15 required significant disclosure — companies must now explain their revenue disaggregation, contract balances (contract assets and contract liabilities / deferred revenue), and significant judgments. The adoption was transformative for technology, telecommunications, real estate, and media companies.

slides.title: Deferred revenue, accrued revenue, and the accounting for subscriptions
slides.body:
Two balance-sheet accounts capture the most common timing differences in revenue recognition:

**Deferred Revenue (Contract Liability / Unearned Revenue).** When a customer pays before the company delivers, the company has a *liability* — the obligation to perform. Until performance occurs, the cash received cannot be recognised as revenue. Examples:
- **Salesforce.com** (now **Salesforce, Inc.**) collects annual SaaS subscription fees upfront — a substantial portion of its balance sheet is deferred revenue. In FY2024, Salesforce reported deferred revenue of approximately $15 billion.
- An airline selling tickets months in advance records deferred revenue; revenue is recognised when the flight occurs.
- A magazine publisher collecting 2-year subscriptions records the cash as deferred revenue and recognises 1/24 per month.

Journal entries for a $1,200 annual subscription paid upfront:
- **At signing**: Debit Cash $1,200 / Credit Deferred Revenue $1,200.
- **Each month (1/12)**: Debit Deferred Revenue $100 / Credit Service Revenue $100.

**Accrued Revenue (Contract Asset / Unbilled Receivable).** Revenue earned but not yet billed or received. A consulting firm that completed work in December but won't invoice until January has earned the revenue — it should be recognised in December under accrual accounting.
- **Adjusting Entry**: Debit Accounts Receivable (or Unbilled Revenue) $X / Credit Service Revenue $X.

**Why this matters economically.** Consider two identical consulting firms, A and B:
- Firm A bills clients immediately upon project completion.
- Firm B bills 60 days after completion.

On December 31, both firms completed the same $500,000 project. Under accrual, both firms record $500,000 in revenue for the year — correctly reflecting equal economic performance. Under cash basis, neither records anything (payment hasn't arrived), and Firm A's December invoice might cause it to *look* better in Q1 of next year when cash arrives. Accrual removes this distortion.

**The FASB and IASB.** The two standard-setters have pursued convergence since the **Norwalk Agreement of 2002**, a memorandum of understanding signed by **Robert Herz** (then FASB chairman) and **Sir David Tweedie** (then IASB chairman) at a meeting in Norwalk, Connecticut. ASC 606 / IFRS 15 is the most successful product of that convergence — the two standards are word-for-word identical in most respects. However, full convergence of US GAAP and IFRS has stalled. The **SEC**, under successive commissioners including **Jay Clayton** and **Gary Gensler**, has declined to mandate IFRS adoption for US domestic issuers, meaning the dual-standard world will persist for the foreseeable future.

**Practical implications for analysts.** When comparing a US company (US GAAP) to a European peer (IFRS), analysts must understand that LIFO inventory accounting (allowed under US GAAP, prohibited under IFRS), asset-revaluation differences, and lease accounting nuances (ASC 842 vs. IFRS 16) can make reported numbers incomparable without adjustment. Revenue recognition under ASC 606 / IFRS 15 is now largely harmonised — but the details of variable consideration, contract modifications, and principal vs. agent determinations still produce differences in application.

question.question: Under ASC 606 / IFRS 15, a software company sells a bundled package: a perpetual software license ($900 standalone selling price) plus one year of technical support ($300 standalone SSP). The customer pays $1,000. How much revenue is recognised at the time the software license is delivered (assuming the license is delivered immediately and support is delivered over 12 months)?
options: $1,000 — all revenue is recognised when the contract is signed and payment received.

$750 — the transaction price is allocated in proportion to standalone selling prices: License SSP = $900 / ($900 + $300) = 75% of total SSP. Allocated to license = $1,000 × 75% = $750. Support = $1,000 × 25% = $250. The $750 allocated to the license is recognised immediately when the license is delivered (a point-in-time obligation). The $250 allocated to support is deferred and recognised ratably over 12 months ($250/12 per month ≈ $20.83/month) as the support service is delivered (an over-time obligation). This is Step 4 (allocate based on SSP) and Step 5 (recognise when each obligation is satisfied) of the five-step ASC 606 / IFRS 15 model.
$900 — the full standalone price of the software is recognised immediately.
$500 — revenue is split equally between the two deliverables.
question.explanation: ASC 606 Step 4 requires allocating the $1,000 transaction price in proportion to standalone selling prices. Total SSP = $900 + $300 = $1,200. License proportion = $900 / $1,200 = 75%; Support = 25%. Allocated amounts: License $750, Support $250. The license is a point-in-time obligation (delivered immediately) — $750 is recognised at delivery. The support is an over-time obligation — $250 is deferred and recognised over 12 months. Recognising $900 (the full SSP of the license) would ignore the discount inherent in the bundle price. Recognising $1,000 upfront would fail to defer the support obligation. Equal split ($500) ignores the SSP allocation requirement entirely.

hints: ASC 606 Step 4: allocate transaction price proportionally to standalone selling prices.
Total SSP = $900 + $300 = $1,200. What % is the license?
slides.workedSolution: Step 4 allocation: License $900 / $1,200 = 75% → $1,000 × 75% = $750. Support $300 / $1,200 = 25% → $1,000 × 25% = $250. Step 5: License delivered at point in time → recognise $750 immediately. Support delivered over 12 months → deferred revenue $250, recognised $250/12 ≈ $20.83 per month. Answer: $750 at delivery.

question.question: A company sells a 12-month software subscription for $3,600, received in full on January 1. By March 31 (end of Q1, three months later), how much **revenue** has been recognised and what is the remaining **Deferred Revenue** balance?
question.hint: Monthly revenue = $3,600 / 12 = $300/month. 3 months × $300 = $900 recognised. Remaining deferred = $3,600 − $900 = $2,700.

question.question: Apply the five-step ASC 606 model to a construction contract
question.goal: A construction company (**BuildRight LLC**) signs a contract to build a warehouse for **Apex Logistics** for $2,000,000. The contract meets all criteria for over-time recognition. At the end of Year 1, BuildRight has incurred costs of $600,000 out of a total estimated cost of $1,500,000. Calculate the percentage of completion, revenue to recognise in Year 1, and the journal entry.

steps.prompt: Identify the performance obligation and confirm whether revenue is recognised at a point in time or over time.
steps.motivation: ASC 606 Step 5 — determine the pattern of recognition.

acceptedAnswers: One performance obligation: construct the warehouse. Recognised over time because the customer controls the asset as it is built and there is no alternative use; over-time recognition.

hints: The customer (Apex) controls the in-progress warehouse. BuildRight has no alternative use for it. These are the over-time criteria.
steps.reveal: Single performance obligation: build the warehouse. Recognition is over time — the customer controls the asset as construction progresses, and BuildRight has no alternative use for a custom warehouse. This is the classic long-term construction contract scenario, historically governed by **IAS 11** (superseded by IFRS 15) and **SOP 81-1** (superseded by ASC 606).

steps.prompt: Calculate the percentage of completion at end of Year 1.
steps.motivation: The cost-to-cost input method is the most common measure of progress.
hints: Percentage complete = Costs incurred to date / Total estimated costs = $600,000 / $1,500,000.
steps.reveal: Percentage of completion = $600,000 / $1,500,000 = **40%**. This is the input (cost-to-cost) method — the most widely used measure of progress under ASC 606 for construction and engineering contracts.

steps.motivation: Revenue recognised = % complete × total contract price.
steps.reveal: Year 1 Revenue = 40% × $2,000,000 = **$800,000**. This is the amount earned in Year 1 based on progress made. Gross profit in Year 1 = Revenue $800,000 − Costs $600,000 = $200,000.

steps.prompt: Record the Year 1 revenue journal entry (assume all billings and cash are handled separately).
steps.motivation: Recognising revenue from a contract asset.

acceptedAnswers: Debit Contract Asset (or Unbilled Revenue) $800,000; Credit Construction Revenue $800,000

hints: Revenue earned but not yet billed creates a Contract Asset (an asset on the balance sheet).
steps.reveal: Journal Entry: **Debit Contract Asset $800,000 / Credit Construction Revenue $800,000**. The Contract Asset represents revenue earned that has not yet been billed to or paid by the customer. When BuildRight bills Apex, the Contract Asset is reclassified to Accounts Receivable. This is the standard over-time recognition journal entry under ASC 606 / IFRS 15.

question.question: Channel stuffing and revenue manipulation
question.prompt: You are an auditor at **Ernst & Young** reviewing the annual financial statements of **SunPower Electronics**, a consumer electronics manufacturer. In Q4, SunPower shipped $15 million of product to its three main distributors — a 60% increase over Q3. The distributors have a **right of return** that expires 90 days after shipment, and SunPower's historical return rate on these distributors is 25%. Management wants to record the full $15 million as revenue in Q4. Using your knowledge of ASC 606 / IFRS 15 (Step 3 variable consideration, Step 5 point-in-time recognition, and the guidance on rights of return), explain: (a) whether the full $15M can be recognised; (b) what adjustments are required; (c) what balance-sheet accounts will be created; and (d) what the pattern of large Q4 shipments to distributors with high return rights might suggest about management's motivations.
